about.title: I turn complex ideas into {accent}
about.p1: For more than 5 years I have been designing and launching high-load corporate and government platforms where a mistake is costly: electronic signatures, role-based access, multi-step forms, heavy dashboards and data visualisation. I also build online stores and landing pages, where load speed, motion and SEO decide the outcome. I take a product from the idea to production — with an architecture (DDD, FSD) that holds up as it grows — and as a Team Lead I answer not only for my own code but for deadlines, reviews and the team.
about.p2: I am as much at home on a blank page as in someone else's code: I have launched products from scratch — from the architecture to the release — and as an outstaffed developer joined other teams, old codebases and systems boxed in on every side. Whatever the conditions, I found a way: not a single contract ended early, I saw every project through to the end and left with the client's thanks.
about.p3: I started before AI assistants existed and learned to design clean, fast and reliable solutions with my own hands. Today AI is part of every stage of my work, and I move many times faster. But it does not think for me — it helps: the architecture, the quality of the code and every decision stay under my control. AI brings the speed; the quality is on me.

skills.title: Where I am strong

core.vue: My main stack since 2021: from a fast SSR site to an enterprise system of dozens of modules. I know not just the API but where the framework saves months and where it starts to get in the way.
core.typescript: Strict types from the API to the button: they are generated from OpenAPI, so a broken contract is caught at build time, not by a user.
core.dataviz: Dashboards, charts and large tables that do not lag; multi-step forms where not a single field gets lost.
core.architecture: I lay down an architecture that grows without a rewrite from scratch, and I lead the team: breaking work down, reviews, releases on schedule.
core.react: My second stack, also in production: fast landing pages with motion, SEO and a headless CMS.

energy.title: Energy Trading Marketplace
energy.about:
A trading marketplace for a regional energy market: local companies buy electricity on it, and generating companies sell it. Procurement lots, commercial bids, auctions and deals, contract registries and reports.

Key business processes are signed with CryptoPro digital signatures, and prices and volumes are shown in complex tables, a market-depth chart and ECharts visualisations.

The project grew out of an old version with heavy tech debt and a Bitrix backend with limited capabilities, and the MVP had to ship in a month and a half, which fell on the New Year holidays.
energy.did:
Came in to own a few modules and ended up leading the whole frontend. The project came from an old version with heavy tech debt, and I reworked its architecture, components and the way it talks to the API
Moved the team to FSD and set a standard for every module: skeletons and clear loading states, a composable of its own for each request
Rewrote the API layer from scratch: interceptors, access middleware, error handling. The old wrapper returned every error with a 200; now the statuses tell the truth
Got the backend to describe its API in Swagger. TypeScript types are generated from OpenAPI on every backend change, and mismatches are caught at build time, not on calls
Brought in Vue Query with caching and deduplication. Every return to a lot page used to fetch all its data again; now it is fetched once, a return opens the page instantly, and the first load takes under a second
Built the lots module from scratch: creating, publishing, editing, withdrawing and signing lots with CryptoPro (together with the backend). Related modules update in real time
Set up document sync between supplier and buyer: about six states per document, and both sides see every change at once
Built multidimensional tables comparing suppliers over long periods: dozens of columns and thousands of rows, loaded lazily, to find the best price fast
As team lead: code reviews that walk through the decisions, mentoring, versioned builds so QA could see exactly what had changed
The MVP shipped on time, though the deadline was cut from 3 months to 1.5 and fell on the New Year holidays. The system runs steadily, and new modules come in without breaking the old ones

education.title: Education Platform
education.about:
A platform for learning and testing knowledge: staff training, interim exams, courses for students. An online school offers it by subscription, under its own brand and on its own platform.

Courses and lessons, a multi-step test builder, a WYSIWYG content editor with maths formulas, events, a calendar with reminders, certificates, chat, course access and five roles with their own rights: student, teacher, curator, administrator and organisation.

The project grew in stages: first an MVP, then new modules as the client brought new tasks. The client supplied its own backend, which at first could not be changed, so much of the logic had to live in the frontend. All of it — the Nuxt frontend, the Node.js backend, PostgreSQL, Redis and MinIO file storage — runs in Docker.
education.did:
Started the project from scratch with a colleague on the DDD architecture he chose. When it only made the product harder to grow, moved it to FSD and migrated from Nuxt 3 to Nuxt 4: features are isolated by layer and do not touch each other, builds and page loads got faster, types stricter
In time the development passed to me entirely: from then on I led and grew the project alone
Built a multi-step test builder: single- and multiple-choice questions and open answers. Every step is saved on the backend, and authoring picks up where it left off
Built a role model of five roles — student, teacher, curator, administrator, organisation — with a hierarchy: senior roles set the rights of the ones under them
Built course access and rights management: payment happens on the client's side, and an administrator opens courses to students through an interface we built
Built a WYSIWYG content editor for courses and lessons on TipTap: formatting, links, fonts and maths formulas in KaTeX
Wrote a complex calendar modelled on Google Calendar: reminders for a course's students with a date, a time, a number of repeats and schedules by day, week and year
Built personal dashboards for every role and an achievements module where teachers award certificates to students
Worked with the client's limited backend: moved its logic into the frontend, carried the changes through every module when it was reworked, and closed tasks on its side myself — Node.js and Ts.ED, TypeORM and PostgreSQL
Where new features had no mockups, designed the interface myself in the client's style
Covered the key flows with tests: unit tests in Vitest and end-to-end tests in Playwright
As team lead: breaking work down, code review, helping the team through the hard parts
The platform is live and in use: organisations and students work in it by subscription

finance.title: Website for a Bitcoin Financial Company
finance.about:
The website of an institutional financial company in the bitcoin space: investment strategies, collateralised lending and onchain products for funds, companies and miners.

About fifteen sections and a resources hub — news, insights, events, reports — with tag filters. The client runs all the content in Sanity. Animation in GSAP and Lottie, analytics through Google Tag Manager, GA4, Microsoft Clarity and HubSpot.

Built by a team of two fullstack developers, a frontend developer and a QA engineer.
finance.did:
Built all of the site's animation in GSAP: smooth reveals, line-by-line text, cascades, waves, parallax
Built a shared Motion component: every animation is set up in one file, so its behaviour changes to the client's wishes without touching the components themselves
Chained the sections' entrances: each page's animations are described in one place, and each one starts halfway through the one before, though the components know nothing of each other
Fixed the client's Lottie animations: the motion designer's files had errors, and we matched the timing of their replays ourselves
In the UI kit, owned breadcrumbs, accordions, sliders, placeholders, inputs, pagination, a custom scroll and the animation component
We split modules by likeness: when one of mine came back on other pages, I owned it everywhere, variants included
Built Sanity right into the Next.js project: the site and the content studio start with one command
Built a Telegram bot for the team: notices of pull requests, deploy statuses and errors
Made the technical decisions on equal terms with the other fullstack developer, and we reviewed each other's code

monitoring.title: Financial Monitoring Portal
monitoring.about:
A budget monitoring portal for a government client: it gathers data from hundreds of organisations across a large region — their budgets and what the money is spent on.

Interactive charts show the trends over chosen periods. A click on any bar drills down into detailed charts, all the way to money flows and single organisations. The rest is large tables for monitoring cash flows.

The portal runs in a closed network and is built to the Russian requirements for government systems: security and accessibility. The backend was rigid and let almost nothing change, so the work went on within very narrow limits. The team was five: three frontend developers, a layout developer and a backend developer.
monitoring.did:
Led a frontend team of four, a layout developer I trained among them: gave out the tasks by each one's strengths, reviewed the code and signed off the work
Took the hardest part myself — dynamic charts written from scratch in plain SVG, with no library
Made the charts responsive and interactive: a click on a bar opens the detailed level, all the way to money flows and single organisations
Built comparisons of the trends across periods
Built authorisation for several role models, each with its own level of access to the data, and data export
Worked within an inflexible backend: whatever the API did not give, I solved on the frontend
Gave the junior developers the tables and page layouts and helped them through their tasks
Brought the portal up to the government client's requirements: a closed network, security and accessibility to the Russian requirements for government systems
Integrated the data through GraphQL

documents.title: Document Management System
documents.about:
A closed internal document management system of a large transport company. It runs in a closed network: only authorised staff with special access can get in, and the whole administrative and management staff works in it.

It holds documents of every format: orders, regulations, reports, technical documentation, contracts. They live in a dynamic tree and are handled through a file explorer right in the browser, as familiar as Windows Explorer: drag and drop, moving through folders, moving files and whole sections. There is a shared exchange where colleagues' files are seen, and a personal space for everyone.

Analytics dashboards in Highcharts show the number of documents, active staff, deadlines and overdue items, certificates. The team was ten: four frontend developers, two backend developers, two QA engineers and two analysts. I joined it when it was falling behind, to speed up the new modules.
documents.did:
Joined the team when it was falling behind and took on new modules
Built a file explorer in the browser that behaves like Windows Explorer: drag and drop, moving through folders, cutting and moving files and whole folders
Built a dynamic document tree: it shows your own files and other users' files, like a shared exchange, and a personal explorer apart from it
Built an analytics dashboard with dynamic charts in Highcharts
At the team's request, helped close its tasks faster: fixed the landing page, rewrote the footer and the sidebar from scratch, strictly to the mockup, pixel perfect: the footer is responsive on every screen, the sidebar works steadily on every device
Handed over all my modules and brought my work on the project to a successful close

processes.title: Business Process Management System
processes.about:
A corporate business process management system for the mining and metals sector: business processes, complex forms, filtering and chat.

Most of the code came from early versions: vanilla JavaScript in ES5 and classes, modules with logic nested up to nine levels deep, where everything was passed down through props. The system reacted badly to any change, the tech debt kept piling up, and new features had to ship at the same time.

The project was moved to a modern approach and TypeScript step by step, module by module. The team was three: a senior developer, me as a middle developer, and a junior developer.
processes.did:
Came to help the senior developer when he could no longer keep up: worked through the tech debt and built new modules side by side
Moved the legacy from ES5 to ES6 and rewrote old components from the Options API to the Composition API and TypeScript — the names, the logic and the structure, from the first line; new modules I wrote with the Composition API and TypeScript from the start
Untangled modules with logic nested up to nine levels deep, where data went down through props alone, and moved them to provide/inject and stores
Fixed broken modules and wrote new ones in a system that reacted badly to any change
Together with the senior developer, caught up with the deadlines and rewrote a huge layer of legacy code

current.desc: Closed the loop: I take a product from the idea to production — the frontend, the backend and a CMS, Docker, CI/CD and deployments. In the team I answer for the technical decisions and the release cycle, from the first line of code to a running service.

energyLead.desc: I led two teams at once: launching a new platform while still developing the earlier one. I answered for the architecture of the key processes, the deadlines and the quality of releases, and through code review and mentoring kept one level of code across both teams.

educationLead.desc: Now I answered not for modules but for a whole product: I started it from scratch, later moved its architecture to FSD, and laid down the rules the team writes code by. I broke the work down, ran code review and did the mentoring of junior developers — that is how the shared standards formed that projects stand on for years.

complexSystems.desc: From doing tasks to owning modules: I carried them whole, from the brief to the release, and agreed the decisions with the team and the backend. I often worked as an outstaffed developer — joining other teams, finding my way through heavy legacy and systems like 1C-Bitrix, where part of the server logic had to live on the frontend. I learned to find a way within any limits. On one project, still a middle developer, I led a frontend team of four.

commercialStart.desc: A first job at an IT company and a new stack: I learned Vue from scratch and still write in it. I took on projects of every kind, including on technologies I had never touched — PHP and Yii2, WordPress, Shopify. I learned from the experienced developers in the team: their reviews quickly turned tasks done by the book into tasks done on my own.

startups.desc: First steps — at home and in small rented offices, in little teams of enthusiasts with startups of their own. I learned frontend on real tasks: markup, JavaScript, my first projects in React. And I learned the main thing: a product is made by a team, not by one developer.

contact.title: Write me a letter
contact.letter: Hello, Daniil. My name is {name}, you can reach me at {contact}. I need help with:
contact.lead: Open to any role, project work and complex product challenges. I answer within a day or two; the quickest way is Telegram or the letter on this page.

form.name: Your name
form.phAbout: a few lines about the project
form.errorName: Name — at least 2 characters, letters only
form.errorContact: Enter a valid email or Telegram — e.g. {email} or {handle}
form.errorContactOwn: Those are my contacts — please leave your own

send.invalid: The letter did not pass the check: look over the name, contact and text, and send it again.
send.delivery: The letter did not get through. Please write to me on Telegram {handle} or at {email}.
send.network: No connection to the server. Check your internet and try again.

form.stackEmpty: Not on the shelf — mention it below
form.consent: I agree to the processing of my name, contact and message so that Daniel can reply. Details are in the {policy}.
form.errorAgree: Tick the consent to data processing — the letter cannot be sent without it

success.text: The letter is sealed · I'll answer within a day or two. If no reply comes, message me directly on Telegram — that way we won't miss each other.
